body: the alcohol wipes and briefcase are wrapped in a child's raincoat. one stayed dry while the other was left in road mud.
title: Alcohol wipes beside the spare mark

body:
Farm diary: the first fire started beneath the assay table after a field sample cracked. The wet soil burned blue before any building caught.

The sample came from the treated plots, and the flame smelled sweet and chemical.
title: First fire under the assay table

body:
Diary entry: beside the second fire mark lay a scorched tray from the soil assay. Its unburned label says the orchard batch was reapplied after rain.

The tray rim was crusted with the same residue as the sprayer nozzles.
title: Second fire, scorched assay tray

body:
Photograph back: the third fire began among returned seed sacks, not the nearby lumber. Violet grains remained in the seams after the flames went out.

The lumber beside them was barely scorched.
title: Third fire, seed sacks first

body:
Farm log: smoke at the fourth fire rose from the rinse pit after the trial crew emptied its hoses. The grass died in a clean ring before dusk.

The pit water still foamed when stirred.
title: Fourth fire beside the rinse pit

body:
Torn notebook page: the fifth fire followed a split treatment drum. Water spread the burning film, so we covered it with field soil and left.

The soil darkened and smoked where the film touched it.
title: Fifth fire after the drum split

body:
Receipt margin: replace two boots burned at the sixth fire on the sampling route. Both soles carried the same sticky amber residue.

The residue stuck to the pencil as I wrote this.
title: Sixth fire on the sample route

body:
Letter draft: the seventh fire caught damp hay where the pasture spray settled. The extension worker asked us to call it a lantern accident.

There was no lantern, only a sprayer parked at the fence.
title: Seventh fire at the hay edge

body:
Diary line: the eighth fire glowed before sunrise around bags from the night application. No homes were burning and no one had run for the road.

The bags were treated seed, split at the seams.
title: Eighth fire before sunrise

body:
Photograph note: the ninth fire follows the drainage cut from the experimental plot. Frogs floated below it while the bank still smoked.

We tried to finish the ordinary work around it. The notice changed faster than the deliveries, and no one came to collect what was left.

It could be a mistake in the copying. The things stacked beside the page were real enough, and still waiting to be moved.
title: Ninth fire by the drainage cut

body:
Maintenance page: the tenth fire blackened the parked sprayer from beneath. The fuel line was intact; dried treatment foam covered the hot shield.

Nobody agreed on whose list this belonged to. I left it where the next person would look for the things we still owed each other.

I could have mistaken the order in which those things happened. I could not mistake the empty place left for the person we had been waiting for.
title: Tenth fire under the sprayer

body:
Personal note: after the eleventh fire, every test cage stood open. The rabbits were gone, but their water pans held white crystals.

The feed trough beside them was dusted with the same crystals.
title: Eleventh fire and empty cages

body:
Farm diary: the twelfth fire consumed only the flagged crop rows. Untreated rows on either side stayed green until the next rain.

The flags carried the trial's plot numbers in marker.
title: Twelfth fire at the row flags

body:
Feed receipt back: at the thirteenth fire we found six empty additive tins behind the shed. The purchase line lists five.

The tins were labelled for crop treatment and still wet inside.
title: Thirteenth fire behind the shed

body:
Notebook sketch: the fourteenth fire crawled across wet ground in the same path as yesterday's trial runoff. Ordinary straw would not burn there.

The runoff had left a slick, yellowish film on the stubble.
title: Fourteenth fire along wet ground

body:
Letter fragment: beneath the fifteenth fire mark I buried a sealed leaf jar. Its leaves spotted black the day after the trial rows were sprayed.

I carried it home because the seed man had no one to return it to. The film from the jar did not come off when I washed my hands.

The next morning I looked for the second jar and found only the lid. I left this one for whoever tends those rows after me.
title: Fifteenth fire and the buried jar

body:
Diary line at the sad face: the field cook wept when three workers could not swallow lunch. All had handled the new grain coating that morning, bare-handed, filling the seed drill.

The coating came in unmarked sacks from the trial supplier. Nobody had told us to wear gloves.

I wrote down who had touched the sacks, in the order they came to the table, while I still remembered.
title: Sad face after the field meal

body:
Photograph back at the first gun: the sick applicator sat on the step beside the sprayer while the sample case stayed locked in the cab. His hands were stained yellow-green to the wrist.

I wrote this on the back because nobody would take a statement about the coating he was spreading. I kept the picture in my coat until my hands stopped shaking.
title: Gun beside the locked sample case

body:
Pay-envelope note at the first happy face: bonus for completing the late spray despite complaints. My hands were numb when I signed.

The foreman drew the smiling face himself, said it meant we had earned it. Two of the crew had already gone home coughing and still got the same envelope, sealed, no questions.

I have not spent it. It is folded inside this note, and I keep telling myself the numbness is only from the cold mornings.
title: Happy face on the bonus sheet

body:
Torn diary page: at the first dead face, stained gloves remained beside a crop-trial badge. The posted list later called the wearer an unknown traveler.

I knew him. He ate at our table twice and talked about the test rows like they were his children. Nobody who knew his name was asked.

I tore this page out so it would not sit with the ordinary days. The badge number is on the back.
title: First dead face, stained gloves

body:
Notebook line: the second dead face marks the well tender who sampled cloudy water for the pasture study. His sample bottle was gone before dawn.

He told me the water smelled sweet, like the drums behind the equipment shed. The pasture beside the well had gone grey-green in a ring where the runoff ran.

The truck was still in his yard. I copied his sample dates from the pump house wall before they painted it.
title: Second dead face by the well

body:
Photograph note: the third dead face lies beside corn that looks untouched. A trial flag was pulled from the row but its wire hole remains, and the stalks beyond it are sprayed pale at the base.

The man beside me recognized the planting pattern and went quiet. Only the rows with flags had been treated.

I did not put this back with the ordinary papers.
title: Third dead face near clean corn

body:
Mileage slip back: the fourth dead face was found on the field truck path. Tire tracks lead away before the road closure begins.

I set it aside to show the neighbor when she returned. Her porch was empty by the time the light was good enough to read it.

The amount mattered to the office more than the people waiting outside. We stayed until dark because the last line still said to wait.
title: Fourth dead face on the truck path

body:
Diary entry: the fifth dead face is beside the crew wash basin. The water smelled of bleach and the rinse ledger had been torn out.

The crew rinsed boots and sprayer hoses here every evening of the trial. I wrote down which hose went with which tank while I could still remember it.

The water below the basin ran yellow into the ditch.
title: Fifth dead face and the wash basin

body:
Torn letter: at the sixth dead face, orchard netting covered a man still wearing sample tags. The fruit above him had split without ripening, all along the sprayed rows.

The trial supervisor wanted a cleaner version of the harvest report. I kept the stained one because it shows which rows were treated and which were not.
title: Sixth dead face under orchard netting

body:
Receipt note: the seventh dead face fell beside feed mixed for the supplement trial. The cart number is absent from the barn account.

The calves that ate from that cart went off their feed within two days. The mix had a sweet chemical smell the plain feed never had.

I kept the receipt because it names the additive.
title: Seventh dead face at the feed cart

body:
Personal map note: the eighth dead face lay beyond the last trial flag, where the wind carried the mist. Officials later measured only inside the flags.

We waited for a correction that never came. Every passing driver had a different instruction and no room for one more passenger.

Perhaps the new instructions were meant to help us. They arrived after we had already followed the old ones.
title: Eighth dead face beyond the flags

body:
Notebook page: a sealed flask beside the ninth dead face contains green field water. The label asks for testing, but no laboratory is named.

I took it from the drainage ditch below the trial plot, where the spray rig was rinsed. The water there had killed the grass along both banks.

I had promised to bring it home for supper. The empty chair at the table and the date on this page now belong to the same evening.
title: Ninth dead face and the sealed flask

body:
Photograph back at the second happy face: the supervisor held up a clean yield sheet while smoke rose behind the trial rows, where the blighted plants were being burned.

Someone said the smell was only from burning stubble. I kept the scrap because the same sweet smell had come from the last field we treated.

The stain is where the first yield figure was crossed out. I have not tried to improve it.
title: Second happy face on a clean report

body:
Diary margin at the second gun: an armed man collected the rinse records and left the seed invoices. He wore no farm badge.

The records were the only list of which tanks had held the coating. The invoices said only what we had bought.

I wrote this down before the next shift, in the order I saw it, and have not tried to improve it.
title: Second gun guarding rinse records

body:
Letter fragment at the second sad face: twelve calf tags came back from the supplement pasture, but only eleven calves were unloaded.

Our copy stayed on the kitchen table. The official account came later and asked us to remember a much shorter day.

I wanted to keep a clean copy, but the stain is where the first entry was crossed out. I have not tried to improve it.
title: Second sad face beside calf tags

body:
Field log at the first skull: this soil core was rejected for a sharp solvent smell. The replacement core came from outside the treated rows.

The rejected core was grey and dry through the root layer, as if the seedlings had been scalded from below.

I took the page when the lab sent back the replacement and it read clean.
title: First skull, rejected soil core

body:
Receipt back at the second skull: one rain-barrel sample, paid cash. The barrel stood downwind of the experimental orchard.

The water in it had a film on top that smelled of the spray. A pencil line on the receipt had been rubbed thin but not erased; I could still read what the sample was meant to be tested for.
title: Second skull, rain-barrel sample

body:
Diary line at the third skull: birds dropped beneath the plot wire after dawn spraying. The crew buried them before opening the gate.

They lay in a line along the treated rows, wings dry and bills stained pale. Nothing had touched them but the mist.

I wrote the number down before the shovels came.
title: Third skull, birds under the wire

body:
Warehouse note at the fourth skull: the returned treatment drum weighed nine pounds less than dispatch. Its seal appeared untouched.

Something had been drawn off at the plot, not at the warehouse; the rim was crusted yellow where a hose had sat.

I wrote the weights side by side. The drum was shipped back out the same afternoon.
title: Fourth skull, missing drum weight

body:
Farm notebook at the fifth skull: pour away milk from the test pasture until told otherwise. The instruction arrived before the cattle looked ill.

The pasture had been sprayed twice that month for the grass trial. The first sick cow came three days after the second pass.

I poured it behind the barn and wrote the dates here.
title: Fifth skull, milk poured away

body:
Photograph back at the sixth skull: bean leaves blackened in the shape of yesterday’s spray fan. The roots remained pale and firm.

No one wanted to keep the wet copy. It dried unevenly, and the ink from the first entry stayed visible beneath the second.

I wrote the time before I went back for the others. The clock may have been slow; the second vehicle was already gone.
title: Sixth skull, blackened bean leaves

body:
Torn ledger at the seventh skull: the final field count omits two applicators and one sample case. Their truck is still marked returned.

Two men sprayed the north rows with the coating and did not come back from them. The truck stood at the field edge with the tank empty.

I saved the page because their names are on the reverse, and not on the crew tally.
title: Seventh skull, final field count
